extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of administrative law and public administration; policymakers interested in tribunal design
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the structure, staffing, powers, procedures, and practical functioning of the Canada Pension Appeals Board (PAB) as established under the CPP, including its origins and distinctive characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational profile and public visibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB has a low public profile: its hearings only attract those directly concerned and it is comparatively little known among federal autonomous agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains causes of low profile: limited subject-matter notoriety compared to bodies like the National Parole Board; hearings attract only directly concerned parties or representatives; recent institution (created 1965) and initially limited activity contributed to modest public standing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency and sporadic character of activity
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB 'sits at irregular intervals and fairly infrequently' and its members are not permanently on duty nor resident near its seat of operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This sporadic activity affects accessibility, continuity, and public awareness; frequency increased only in early 1970s, but overall tempo remains modest compared to other agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory composition and numerical membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership is summarily defined by subsection 85(2) of the CPP; originally could vary between three and six persons; a 1974 amendment created a Vice-Chairman and increased membership to a maximum of ten persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details include requirement that the Chairman be appointed from among judges of the Exchequer Court (Federal Court) or superior provincial courts; Vice-Chairman also must be chosen from Federal Court or superior courts; quorum implications (see separate entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial background of members
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB is constituted of judges (provincial and federal) — e.g., Chairman and other members drawn from ordinary courts rather than administrative specialists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointment of judges was intended to give prestige and credibility; practical consequences include part-time commitment, judges not specialists in administrative law or social security, and subordination to their courts' calendars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language (bilingual) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Language requirements under the Official Languages Act further restrict recruitment; most members are bilingual or have attained sufficient competence in both official languages since appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the tribunal frequently hears unrepresented ordinary citizens with limited ability to express themselves, linguistic aptitudes of members are of special importance; appointments have been used to ensure regional and linguistic representation (e.g., French-speaking minorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remuneration and emoluments
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the PAB receive no emoluments by reason of their office; their only remuneration is that attached to their usual duties under the Judges Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: members serve part-time without separate pay, which affects availability and incentive structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provincial consultation and regional representation
rubrics_metrics.description: When PAB served as QPP Review Commission, Quebec was to be consulted on the choice of certain members; appointments aim to make collegial administrative bodies representative of geographical regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical arrangements (federal-provincial negotiations) affected appointments; representation of Quebec and French-speaking minorities noted as deliberate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part-time service and its operational consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Members are not permanently on duty; each spends a maximum of 8 weeks per annum at sittings and maintain usual residence in various provinces, causing travel demands and constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include delays, scheduling difficulties, risk of slowing down the process of justice, and inability to reconstitute the same bench quickly after adjournments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chairman powers and responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chairman's principal powers are detailed under section 85 of the CPP: arranging sittings/hearings, presiding over sittings, giving or refusing leave to appeal in matters of benefits, granting extensions of time for appealing, requiring production of documents, ordering preliminary examinations of witnesses, delegating cross-examination of affidavit witnesses, and coordinating PAB work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some powers apply to the Board generally; others are exclusive (e.g., under QPP the power to extend time is the Chairman's exclusive prerogative). The Chairman's organizational responsibility (coordination) implies a need for assistance (Registrar). Certain procedural powers and their limits are discussed further in chapter 4 (leave to appeal, time limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave to appeal and time-limit powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for leave to appeal vary by jurisdiction; the Chairman and Vice-Chairman have the power of giving or refusing leave to appeal in matters of benefits, and have authority to grant extensions of time for appealing (normal period is 90 days except where law provides no time-limit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifics: 90 days from communication or transmission by mail for appeals (except unemployment insurance where no time-limit); in CPP power to extend time pertains both to Board as a whole and to each member severally; in QPP power is exclusive to Chairman. These powers are incident to procedural control and have significant effects on parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registrar duties and case-management role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Registrar's duties are not expressly defined in the CPP but in practice the Registrar is the chief auxiliary officer, charged with collecting all documents, notifying parties of decisions, informing the Chairman of applications, transmitting notices and replies, informing parties of hearing times/places, notifying withdrawals/interventions/incidental applications/decisions, ordering production of documents, issuing subpoenas, summoning witnesses, recording/registering decisions, and preserving records of hearings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registrar organizes hearings, prepares case-files, follows appeal process through phases, has custody of Review Committee records for possible second appeal, and must balance informing the public with remaining an impartial officer (risk of being seen as legal advisor). Registrar and staff paid out of Department budget but assigned exclusively to PAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical facilities and administrative support
rubrics_metrics.description: Headquarters in Ottawa with a mailing address in Montreal for QPP matters; permanent offices at Department of National Health and Welfare; facilities consist of Registrar's office and additional office space; technical support (mail, telephone, telex, supplies, photocopy) provided by the Department; no other premises reserved elsewhere in Canada.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of dedicated premises elsewhere contributes to complexity of organizing hearings across the country and dependence on Departmental support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hearing location principle and proximity to appellant
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of hearing location guided by the generally observed principle that in litigation between a member of the public and an administrative authority the adjudicating tribunal must hold its hearing as close as possible to the residence of the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CPP recognizes corollary right to compensation for expenses and loss of earnings for persons summoned; no such provision in QPP, so PAB makes special effort to locate QPP hearings near appellants. Practical constraints (member availability, travel difficulties, remoteness) impede mobility and tend to favor city-dwelling appellants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity of hearings (public vs in camera)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule PAB hearings are public, at least in matters relating to benefits; under exceptional circumstances the Board may decide to sit in camera; publicity is also the rule in matters of contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction between benefits and contributions is difficult to justify because private information may arise in either (income, business finances, health, marital relations). Privacy concerns can justify in camera sittings in exceptional cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quorum requirement and its practical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Quorum is set at three members; this requirement creates administrative complications and delays because assembling three already-busy judges from different provinces for several days is difficult; the PAB has seldom sat with more than three members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequences include long waits after adjournments if same judges cannot be reassembled, tendency to postpone hearings unlikely to yield final decision within scheduled time, and that the root problem is members' part-time status rather than quorum per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling logistics and 'circuit' hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Registrar must make hearing calendars taking into account number of appeals from a region, dates filed, state of files, availability of sufficient PAB members, travel and accommodation, availability of parties/counsel/witnesses, and may organize circuits—carefully-scheduled sittings enabling liquidation of a region's accumulated business within a week or two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizing hearings is complex because PAB has no premises nor full-time members; Registrar sometimes shares travel inconvenience by locating hearings midway between scattered parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financing, departmental administrative arrangements, and cost-sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Administratively the PAB is an appendage of the Department of National Health and Welfare; budgets for Registrar and staff and hearing-organizing expenses (notably travel) are assumed by the Department. An agreement with Quebec fixed Quebec's percentage share of operating costs on pro rata basis (77:23 CPP:QPP beneficiaries for a specified period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical cost-sharing arrangements arose from federal-provincial negotiations; transfer of QPP benefit jurisdiction may alter Quebec's participation; financing arrangement economizes on facilities but raises questions of appropriateness when PAB handles matters under other departments (e.g., Unemployment Insurance) and of fairness in cost allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origins and absence of a clear institutional model
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB was an original creation with no identifiable Canadian or American model; though inspired to some degree by the American scheme, it departs significantly (e.g., appointment of provincial judges) and is sui generis among autonomous federal agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative choice of forms has been random; PAB evolved pragmatically rather than from coherent legislative policy or faithful emulation of another country's tribunal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal nature: autonomous administrative agency versus judicial tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB exhibits characteristics of an autonomous administrative agency (independence and specialization) and resembles a court of justice, yet the PAB itself has described its nature as judicial rather than administrative, intending to act 'in the normal unfettered and independent manner of judges.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This duality affects expectations about procedures, standards of fairness and impartiality, and how PAB members perceive their role; statutory wording, composition of judges, and self-characterization inform debates on whether PAB should be treated as judicial or administrative for procedural and normative purposes.
